meta.title: {clinic} — dental clinic in Vlorë, Albania
meta.description: Complete dental care in Vlorë: check-ups, fillings, root canal treatment, crowns and implants. A written treatment plan and the price agreed at the first visit.

cta.title: Come and have it looked at.
cta.body: Tell us what is bothering you and we will ring you back during opening hours. Nothing is started before you have the plan in writing and the price agreed.

treatments.metaDescription: Every treatment at our practice in Vlorë — check-ups, fillings, root canal treatment, crowns, veneers, extractions, oral surgery, implants, dentures, braces and whitening — with how many appointments each one takes and how long it keeps you here.
treatments.title: {count} treatments, and what each one asks of you.
treatments.lede: The same {count} the front page lists, with the part that would not fit on a card: what actually happens, how many appointments it takes, and how many days it keeps you in Vlorë.

detail.checkup: It takes about half an hour. We look at every tooth and at the gums around them, take a radiograph where there is something that cannot be seen from the outside, and clean off what a toothbrush cannot reach. You leave with a plan in the order things matter — what needs doing now, what can wait, and what only needs watching.
detail.fillings: The decayed part is removed and the tooth is rebuilt in a composite matched to the shade of your own enamel, layer by layer, and set hard with a lamp. It is done under local anaesthetic and you can eat as soon as you leave. A tooth treated early is a filling; the same tooth left alone becomes a root canal.
detail.rootCanal: When decay reaches the nerve the tooth is not lost — the canals are cleaned out, shaped and sealed to the tip of the root. It is done under anaesthetic, and it is the treatment that ends the pain rather than the one that causes it. A back tooth is usually crowned afterwards, because what is left of it is thinner than it was.
detail.crowns: A crown is made in a laboratory from an impression or a scan and covers what is left of the tooth. It is tried in before it is cemented, and the shade is chosen against the teeth either side of it rather than out of a catalogue. A bridge is the same work carrying a false tooth across a gap.
detail.veneers: A layer of porcelain about as thick as a fingernail, made in the laboratory and bonded to the front of the tooth. It is what we reach for when the colour will not come back with whitening, or when a tooth is small, worn or chipped. Very little enamel is removed, and in some cases none at all — but what is removed does not grow back, so which of the two your case is gets said before the work starts rather than after.
detail.extraction: Sometimes there is nothing left worth saving, and a wisdom tooth is more often in the way than in trouble. It is done under local anaesthetic, and what matters as much as the extraction itself is what you do for the two days after it — which you get in writing rather than said at the door.
detail.oralSurgery: The surgical work that takes more than a straightforward extraction: wisdom teeth still under the gum or inside the bone, fractured roots, and adding bone when what you have will not hold an implant. It is done under local anaesthetic and planned from an X-ray beforehand rather than worked out as it goes. You leave with written instructions and a review appointment already booked.
detail.implants: A titanium root is placed where the missing one was and then left alone while the bone grows onto it — that is the wait, and it is the part no clinic can shorten. Months later the crown goes on top. It is the only treatment here that replaces the root as well as the tooth, which is why the teeth either side of the gap are left untouched.
detail.dentures: When too many teeth are gone for a bridge, a denture replaces them and rests on the gums or on the teeth that remain. It is built in stages — impression, bite, a try-in in wax, then the finished one — and the wax try-in is there precisely so you can see the shape and the colour and change them while nothing has been cut. It takes more appointments than anything else on this page, and the first weeks are practice: speaking and eating with it is a habit that arrives.
detail.orthodontics: Fixed braces or clear aligners, depending on how far the teeth have to move and what you are willing to wear while they do it. You see the plan before the first bracket is fitted. It is the one treatment here measured in months rather than days, and most of those months are spent at home rather than in the chair.
detail.whitening: In the chair in one appointment, or with trays made for you to use at home over a week or two. It lifts the colour out of the enamel and takes nothing off it. Crowns and fillings do not change shade, so anything at the front is matched afterwards rather than before.

practice.metaDescription: Dr. Votim Shehu's practice in Vlorë: how the first visit goes, the rooms and the equipment in photographs, how the records are kept, and the three languages the practice works in.
practice.title: A practice that writes everything down.
practice.lede: Who does the work, what happens in the first hour, and the two things that are true of every appointment here whatever you came in for.

first.title: Your first visit, step by step.
first.lede: It is the appointment people put off the longest, so here is the whole of it before you book. Nothing on this list is done to you without being explained first.

listen.title: You tell us what brought you in
listen.body: Before anything is looked at. If it has been years, say so — it is the most common reason people come, and nobody here is going to make a point of it.

examine.title: A full examination
examine.body: Every tooth and the gums around them, and a radiograph where there is something that cannot be seen from the outside. It takes about half an hour and none of it hurts.

record.title: What we found, tooth by tooth
record.body: Written into your chart as we go, per tooth rather than as a paragraph — so what was found today is in front of us at the next visit, and at the one after that.

plan.title: The plan, and the price
plan.body: In writing, in the order things matter: what needs doing now, what can wait, and what only needs watching. The price is agreed here rather than at the end.

decide.title: You decide
decide.body: Nothing is started at the first visit unless you want it started. Take the plan away, think about it, ring us back — it stays on your record either way.

languages.title: Three languages, no interpreter.
languages.lede: A treatment plan explained through a relative on a video call is how somebody ends up agreeing to work they did not understand. Everything here — the examination, the plan, the instructions for afterwards — happens in whichever of these three you are most comfortable in.
languages.sq: The practice's own language, and the one the records are kept in.
languages.en: For patients from the UK and Ireland, and for everybody who lands somewhere in between.
languages.it: A short flight from the other side of the Adriatic, and a good share of our patients make it.

clinic.title: What makes the trip worth it.
clinic.lede: Four things that are true of every appointment at this practice, whether you live two streets away or landed this morning.

plan.title: The plan and the price, in writing
plan.body: You leave the first visit knowing what is to be done, how many appointments it takes and what it costs. It does not change along the way without being said out loud.

languages.title: Albanian, Italian, English
languages.body: The work is explained in the language you think in. No interpreter and no nodding along — which matters most in the appointment where you are being asked to decide something.

record.title: An electronic record, tooth by tooth
record.body: Your chart is kept per tooth, so what was found last year is on the screen this year. If you are treated here across two trips, the second starts where the first stopped.

clean.title: Sterilised between patients
clean.body: Instruments are cleaned, packed and sterilised after every use, and single-use items are exactly that. It is the floor rather than a feature — but it is the question people are too polite to ask.

hours.lede: These seven rows are the practice's own hours, read from the same place the appointment book reads them. Change the surgery's hours and this page has already changed.
hours.caption: Opening hours, Monday to Sunday
hours.note: Open does not mean free. The hours here are when somebody is at the desk; which of those hours are still unbooked is what the booking page asks about.

abroad.metaDescription: Dental treatment in Vlorë for patients travelling from Italy, the UK and further: how many appointments and how many days each treatment takes, the three ways into the city, and what happens once you have flown home.
abroad.title: The journey, and what comes after it.
abroad.lede: How many appointments each treatment takes and how many days that keeps you here, the three ways into Vlorë, and what the practice does once you have gone home again.

getting.title: Three ways into Vlorë.
getting.lede: A good share of the people who sit in this chair did not start the day in Albania. Tell us how you are travelling and when you arrive, and the appointments are fitted around the journey rather than the other way about.

air.title: By air
air.body: Tirana is the international airport most patients fly into, and the road down to the coast is the usual way in from there. Send us your flight and we will tell you what can realistically be done on the day you arrive and what is better left to the morning after.

sea.title: By sea
sea.body: There are ferry crossings between Italy and the Albanian coast, and several of our Italian patients come this way rather than fly. Routes change from one summer to the next, so check the operator's own timetable — and tell us which crossing you are on.

road.title: By road
road.body: Vlorë is on the coast road, and patients drive in from Tirana, from the south and from the Greek border. If you are coming a long way for a first appointment, write to us before you set off rather than after.

getting.bayCaption: Vlorë sits on the bay. It is the one photograph on this site genuinely taken here, which is why it is used where the page talks about travelling rather than as decoration.

city.title: Vlorë, if you have never been.
city.lede: A working port on the Albanian coast, and the town this practice has always been in. Most patients who fly in make a few days of it rather than turning straight round.

seas.title: Where two seas meet
seas.body: Vlorë sits at the point the Adriatic gives way to the Ionian. It is why the water changes colour halfway down the bay, and why the coast south of the town looks nothing like the coast north of it.

history.title: Where the country began
history.body: Albania declared its independence here, in 1912, and the town has the flag, the square and the museum to say so. If you have an afternoon between appointments, the old town and the waterfront are within a walk of each other.

riviera.title: The Riviera starts above the town
riviera.body: The coast road climbs out of Vlorë and over the pass, and the beaches people mean when they say the Albanian Riviera are on the other side of it. It is the stretch worth a spare day, if you have one.

city.note: None of this is why anybody chooses a dentist, and it is not offered as though it were. It is here because a first appointment abroad is a trip as well as a treatment, and it is fair to know what the place is.

book.title: Tell us when suits you.
book.lede: The calendar on this page is our own week, read from the same rows the surgery is run from. Nothing is booked by choosing a day: it is what we ring you back about.

treatment.stepsLede: The three steps every treatment here has: what is looked at first, what happens in the chair, and what you leave with.
treatment.timingLede: Appointments, days in Vlorë, and months from start to finish.
treatment.relatedLede: Not a sales list — what most often goes with this, or the other honest answer to the same problem.
treatment.lookLede: The chair, the instruments, the bench behind them and the people who use them — the part of a treatment a paragraph cannot show you.

one.title: The look
one.body: Every tooth, the gums around them, and an X-ray wherever something does not show from the outside.

two.title: The clean
two.body: Scale and staining come off with ultrasonics, including where the brush never reaches.

three.title: The plan
three.body: You leave with the order of work: what now, what can wait, and what is only kept under watch.

one.title: Anaesthetic
one.body: Only the tooth being worked on, and we wait until you feel nothing.

two.title: Clearing the decay
two.body: All of the affected part comes out; what is left underneath is sound tooth.

three.title: Rebuilding
three.body: Composite goes in layer by layer in the shade of your enamel and is cured. You can eat as soon as you leave.

one.title: Diagnosis
one.body: The X-ray shows how far the infection has gone and how many canals the tooth has.

two.title: Cleaning the canals
two.body: Under anaesthetic. The canals are cleaned, shaped and sealed to the tip of the root.

three.title: Covering it
three.body: The tooth is closed, and on a back tooth a crown usually follows it.

one.title: Preparation
one.body: The tooth is shaped and an impression or a scan taken; you leave with a temporary crown.

two.title: The laboratory
two.body: The crown is made in porcelain or zirconia, and the shade is chosen against the teeth beside it.

three.title: Try-in and fit
three.body: It is tried before it is cemented. If the bite or the colour does not convince, it goes back.

one.title: Agreeing the shape
one.body: Colour and shape are settled together, and how much enamel comes off is said beforehand.

two.title: Impression and laboratory
two.body: The veneers are made in porcelain on your own impression, not from a stock shell.

three.title: Bonding
three.body: Tried one at a time, then bonded. You bite normally from that day.

one.title: The X-ray
one.body: The root and what sits around it are seen before anything is touched.

two.title: The extraction
two.body: Under local anaesthetic. You feel pressure, not pain; if you feel pain, we stop.

three.title: The first two days
three.body: The instructions come in writing, and a number to call if something is not right.

one.title: Planning
one.body: The X-ray shows where the tooth is or how much bone there is, and the work is settled before it starts.

two.title: The procedure
two.body: Local anaesthetic, one appointment. It takes longer than a simple extraction, not worse.

three.title: Review
three.body: Stitches and healing are looked at in an appointment booked before you leave.

one.title: Will the bone hold it
one.body: The X-ray shows how much bone there is. If there is not enough, grafting comes first.

two.title: Placing it
two.body: The titanium root goes in under local anaesthetic, and then the bone is given time.

three.title: The crown
three.body: Three to six months later the crown goes on top. That is the second visit, usually the second trip.

one.title: Impression and bite
one.body: The shape of the gums and the way the jaws close are both recorded.

two.title: The wax try-in
two.body: You see it and try it before anything is final. Changes happen here.

three.title: Fitting and adjustment
three.body: It is fitted, then adjusted after the first week; sore spots are expected rather than a surprise.

one.title: The plan
one.body: Impressions, photographs and an X-ray, then the route the teeth will take — before the first bracket goes on.

two.title: The movement
two.body: Fixed braces or aligners, with a check every few weeks. Most of it happens away from the chair.

three.title: The retainer
three.body: When it is finished, the retainer is what holds it. Without one they drift slowly back.

one.title: The check first
one.body: Whitening is not done over decay or inflamed gums; those are dealt with first.

two.title: The whitening
two.body: In the clinic within one appointment, or with trays made for you to take home.

three.title: Keeping it
three.body: The new shade is measured and recorded. Crowns and fillings do not whiten, so they are matched afterwards.

hero.lede: Complete dental care in Vlorë — a precise diagnosis, a treatment plan in writing, and the price agreed at the first visit.
hero.ledeShort: “Be true to your teeth, and they won't be false to you.”

treatments.title: The work, shown rather than hidden.
treatments.lede: From the next check-up to an implant. For each one we tell you how many visits it takes and what it costs — before we start, not at the end.

checkup.title: Check-up and hygiene
checkup.body: A full examination, a scale and polish, and a plan in the order things matter. Everything starts here.

fillings.title: Fillings
fillings.body: The decay comes out and the tooth goes back to its own shape, in a composite matched to your enamel.

rootCanal.title: Root canal treatment
rootCanal.body: The canals are cleaned and sealed to the tip of the root. The tooth stays yours.

crowns.title: Crowns and bridges
crowns.body: When little of the tooth is left, a crown covers what remains. Made in the laboratory and tried in before it is fitted.

veneers.title: Veneers
veneers.body: Thin porcelain shells over the front of the tooth. The shape and the colour change; the tooth underneath stays.

extraction.title: Extractions
extraction.body: When there is nothing left to save, wisdom teeth included. Under anaesthetic, with clear instructions for afterwards.

oralSurgery.title: Oral surgery
oralSurgery.body: Teeth still buried in bone, broken roots, and the bone an implant needs first. Local anaesthetic, one appointment.

implants.title: Implants
implants.body: A titanium root where the missing one was, and a crown on top of it. The closest thing to the tooth you had.

dentures.title: Dentures
dentures.body: A full or partial denture where too many teeth are missing for a bridge. Tried in wax before anything is final.

orthodontics.title: Orthodontics
orthodontics.body: Fixed braces or clear aligners. The teeth move slowly into place, and you see the plan before the first one is fitted.

whitening.title: Whitening
whitening.body: In the chair, or with trays to take home. It takes nothing off the enamel — it gives back the colour you had.

concerns.title: What brings you in?

missing.label: A tooth is missing
missing.body: A gap changes how you bite and how the teeth either side of it sit. It can be filled with an implant — a new root with a crown on top — or bridged from the teeth beside it. Which one suits you depends on the bone underneath, and that is what the first visit looks at.

pain.label: Something hurts
pain.body: Pain is what we see soonest. Most of it is decay that has reached the nerve, and it is treated either with a filling or, once the nerve is involved, by cleaning and sealing the root. Ring us rather than waiting — it does not settle on its own.

looks.label: I do not like how they look
looks.body: Sometimes it is the colour and sometimes the shape. Whitening gives back the colour the enamel had and takes nothing off it; where a tooth is chipped or worn, a crown restores the shape. We tell you which is enough before anything is started.

crooked.label: My teeth are crooked
crooked.body: Fixed braces or clear aligners, depending on how far the teeth have to move and what you want to wear while they do it. You see the plan and the finishing position before the first one is fitted.

gums.label: My gums bleed
gums.body: Bleeding when you brush is usually the first sign of gum disease, and at that stage it can still be turned around. It starts with a full examination and a scale — not with treating the teeth themselves.

overdue.label: It has been years
overdue.body: That is the most common reason people come, and nobody here is going to make a point of it. A first appointment is an examination, a scale and polish, and a written plan in the order things matter — not a list of everything at once.

practice.bodyTwo: We work in Albanian, Italian and English — no interpreter and no misunderstandings, including if you are flying in for the treatment.

record.title: Written down, tooth by tooth

visit.travelBody: A good share of our patients fly in from Italy and the UK. Write to us before you travel: we will tell you how many visits it takes, how many days it keeps you here and what it costs — before you buy the ticket.
visit.bookTitle: Pick a day, and we ring you back.
visit.bookBody: Our own calendar is on the booking page — the days it offers are days the practice is open. Choose one, leave a number, and we agree the hour on the telephone.

trip.lede: Tick what you are asking about and we will show how many appointments it takes, how many days it keeps you in Vlorë, and whether that is one trip or two.
trip.empty: Tick a treatment and the estimate appears here.
trip.oneTrip: One trip. Everything here is done in a single stay.
trip.twoTrips: Two trips. The first places the work, then it needs time to heal before the second finishes it.
trip.caveat: An indication, not a quote. What it actually takes depends on the examination — and you get the plan, how many visits, how long and what it costs, in writing at the first visit.
trip.pricesReviewed: Prices last checked {date}. The figure agreed at your first visit is the one that counts.

aftercare.title: And when you have flown home.
aftercare.lede: It is the question that decides whether somebody books at all, and the one a website usually leaves out. Nothing here is promised for the occasion — it is what the practice already does, written down.

instructions.title: Written instructions before you leave
instructions.body: What to do, what to avoid and for how long — on paper, in the language you were treated in. Not a leaflet in Albanian handed to somebody who does not read Albanian.

checkIn.title: We write to you a few days later
checkIn.body: A message asking how you are getting on, sent from the practice's own follow-up board rather than left to somebody remembering. If anything hurts or does not feel right, you reply to it and we take it from there.

record.title: Your record goes where you go
record.body: Kept electronically, tooth by tooth, with the plan and what was actually done. Ask for it and it is sent — to you, or to a dentist at home who needs to know what is in your mouth.

wrong.title: If something is wrong, say so early
wrong.body: Ring or write, in whichever of the three languages you were treated in. The practice's own follow-up message ends on exactly that offer and means it: we would far rather hear about it early than at your next check-up.

reminders.whatsappTemplate: Hello {name}, this is a reminder of your dental appointment on {date} at {time}. See you soon!
reminders.emailBody:
Hello {name},

This is a friendly reminder of your dental appointment on {date} at {time}.

If you need to reschedule, just reply to this email or call us.

Kind regards,
The dental clinic
reminders.recallWhatsapp: Hello {name}, it has been {months} months since your last check-up. Would you like to book an appointment? We would be glad to see you.
reminders.recallEmailBody:
Hello {name},

Our records show your last visit was {last}. A check-up every few months keeps small problems small.

Just reply to this email or call us to book a time that suits you.

Kind regards,
The dental clinic
reminders.followUpWhatsapp: Hello {name}, it has been {days} days since your treatment. How are you feeling? Let us know if anything is bothering you.
reminders.followUpEmailSubject: How are you feeling after your treatment?
reminders.followUpEmailBody:
Hello {name},

It has been {days} days since we treated you ({services}). We wanted to check how you are getting on.

If anything is painful or does not feel right, reply to this email or call us and we will see you.

Kind regards,
The dental clinic
reminders.waitlistWhatsapp: Hello {name}, a slot has opened up on {day} at {time}. Would you like it? Let us know and we will hold it for you.
reminders.confirmAsk: Please let us know if you are coming: {link}
reminders.workWhatsapp: Hello {name}, your {work} has arrived back from the laboratory. Would you like to come in and have it fitted? Let us know a time that suits you.
reminders.workEmailBody:
Hello {name},

Your {work} has come back from the laboratory and is ready for you.

Reply to this email or call us and we will find a time that suits you.

Kind regards,
The dental clinic
reminders.planWhatsapp: Hello {name}, there is still a step of your treatment to do — {step}. Would you like to book it? We are happy to find a time that suits you.
reminders.planWhatsappPlain: Hello {name}, your treatment ({plan}) is not finished yet. Would you like to book the next appointment?

Hello {name},

Your treatment plan ({plan}) still has a step to go — {step} — and it has been a while since we saw you for it.

There may be a good reason, and if so just tell us. Otherwise, reply to this email or call us and we will find a time.

Kind regards,
The dental clinic

Hello {name},

The first digit is the quadrant, the second is how far back the tooth sits. So 26 is the upper-left sixth tooth — the first molar. Charts are always stored this way, even when the labels are set to the American 1–32.

roles.title: What each role may do
labels: Book appointments
Open the dental chart
See statistics
Staff and log

The answers do not simply narrow down the list. A locum reads the chart and the figures and changes nothing; the front desk books all day and never opens a chart. Deleting anything is the owner’s alone.

expiry.title: Lots against today
labels: Today
Already expired
Turning soon
Fine for now

day.title: What a working day is made of
labels: Booked
Closed — outside opening hours, or the lunch break
Free and bookable
The grey comes from Opening hours. Change the week there and every screen that draws a day follows.

order.title: How an order runs its course
labels: A material drops to or below its minimum and joins the suggested order
The order is placed with the supplier and recorded here
Boxes arrive — in one delivery or several — and the order counts down
Nothing is still owed, and the order closes itself

dashboard.title: Dashboard
dashboard.tagline: The five minutes at the start of the day
dashboard.what: The screen to open first thing and again last thing. It gathers what today actually needs — who is coming, what has not been written up, what the storage room is short of — so none of it has to be remembered or hunted for.

steps.title: The counts across the top
steps.body: Patients on file, today’s and this week’s bookings, recalls due and materials below their minimum. Each one opens the list behind it.

steps.title: Quick actions
steps.body: Add a patient or book an appointment without leaving this screen — the same forms the calendar uses.

steps.title: What needs attention
steps.body: Stock alerts, recalls and requests from the website. On a good day these panels are empty, and that is exactly what they are for.

steps.title: Today’s schedule
steps.body: Every appointment today in order, with its status. Press a row to open the patient.

steps.title: Free time
steps.body: The gaps left in today. Press one to book straight into it when somebody rings asking for “anything this afternoon”.

dashboard.example: It is 08:40. The dashboard says three appointments today, two recalls due and one material low. You press the low material, see it is the anaesthetic, and ring the supplier before the first patient arrives at nine.
tips: An empty panel is not a broken panel — it means nothing is waiting.
Come back at the end of the day. “Treated, not written up” catches the visit notes nobody had time for at the chair.

appointments.title: Calendar
appointments.tagline: The practice’s day, week and month
appointments.what: Everything the practice has agreed to do, and when. The day is built and rebuilt here — bookings are made, moved, marked as arrived and closed off on this screen.

steps.title: Day, week, month or list
steps.body: Four ways of looking at the same bookings. The week is for planning, the day is for working, the list is for finding.

steps.title: Moving through time
steps.body: The arrows step back and forward and “Today” comes home. Filter by dentist or by chair alongside.

steps.title: The grid
steps.body: Hours the practice is shut are greyed out, taken from Opening hours. Drag a booking to move it to another slot.

steps.title: A booking
steps.body: Press it for the patient, the treatment and the notes — then mark them arrived, completed, or a no-show.

steps.title: Free time
steps.body: Double-click empty space to book it. The form says if the slot clashes with another booking or overruns the gap.

appointments.example: A patient rings on Tuesday to move Thursday’s filling. Open the week, drag the block from Thursday to Friday morning, and say why it is moving — the record keeps the new time and the reason together.
tips: An appointment that was never closed off makes the no-show figure wrong. The dashboard lists them so they can be settled honestly.
Breaks, closures and holidays all come from Opening hours. Change them there and this grid follows.

daySheet.title: Day sheet
daySheet.tagline: Today, on one sheet of paper
daySheet.what: The day printed: every appointment in order with the patient, the treatment and a box to tick. For the surgery wall, the trolley, or anybody who would rather work off paper than a screen.

steps.title: The day it shows
steps.body: Today by default. It follows whichever day you came from on the calendar.

steps.title: The rows
steps.body: Time, patient, treatment — in the order they will happen, so the sheet reads like the day does.

steps.title: What is still free
steps.body: The gaps are listed under the bookings, so the sheet answers “can we fit somebody in” without a screen.

steps.title: Print
steps.body: Prints clean: no menus, no search box, no colour to waste.

daySheet.example: Friday morning the printer runs one copy for the surgery and one for the front desk. The nurse ticks each patient off as they leave, and nothing gets lost between the chair and the computer.
tips: The sheet is a snapshot. A booking made after it was printed will not be on it — print again after a busy morning.

patients.title: Patients
patients.tagline: Everybody the practice has on file
patients.what: The list of people, searched by name, telephone or email. It is the way in to a record: the chart, the plans, the visits, the files and the prescriptions all hang off one person here.

steps.title: Search
steps.body: Type any part of a name, a number or an address. Accents do not matter — “cesh” finds “Çeshtje”.

steps.title: New patient
steps.body: A name and a telephone number are enough. Everything else can be filled in later, or never.

steps.title: A row
steps.body: Press it to open the whole record. The row itself shows age, telephone and when they were last seen.

steps.title: The badges
steps.body: A red badge means a recorded allergy or medical alert. It is drawn on the list so it is seen before the chair, not after.

steps.title: The row menu
steps.body: Book, message or edit without opening the record — for when the person is on the telephone and waiting.

patients.example: A woman rings and says only “it’s Marku, about my daughter”. Type mark into the search box: both Markus appear with their ages, and the eight-year-old is obviously the one.
tips: Two records for the same person happen. There is a merge on the record itself that joins them without losing either history.
Setting a recall interval on the record is what puts somebody on the recall list later. Left as “Never”, they are never chased.

patientRecord.title: A patient’s record
patientRecord.what: Everything the practice knows about one person, in tabs: who they are, their dental chart, what has been done, what is planned, their appointments, their files and their prescriptions.

steps.title: The header
steps.body: Name, age, telephone — and any allergy or medical alert in red, on every tab, so it cannot be missed.

steps.title: The tabs
steps.body: Details, chart, visits, plans, appointments, files, prescriptions and contact. Each is a different question about the same person.

steps.title: The dental chart
steps.body: Press a tooth to record its condition, its surfaces, pocket depths and a note. A finding here can be turned straight into a treatment plan.

steps.title: Visit history
steps.body: What was actually done, on which day, by whom. Written after treatment — this is the clinical record and it is what the audit log signs.

steps.title: Record a visit
steps.body: The button that closes the loop: it writes the note, spends the materials used, and can offer the prescription that usually follows.

steps.title: Contact, appointments and files
steps.body: The tabs the front desk lives in: how to reach them and whether they agreed to be messaged, everything they have booked, and their documents.

patientRecord.example: Decay is charted on tooth 26. The chart offers to put a filling on the treatment plan; you accept, the step arrives carrying the tooth number, and when it is booked the appointment is already named.
tips: Medical notes and the chart are hidden from roles that may not see them. A receptionist gets the same record without the clinical half.
Files accept photographs, x-rays and PDFs — including both sides of an identity card, which the front desk can check without opening the file list.

plans.title: Treatment plans
plans.tagline: Every course of treatment the practice has going
plans.what: A plan is an agreed course of treatment broken into steps. This screen is all of them at once, worst-neglected first, so nothing that was agreed quietly stops happening.

steps.title: Search and filter
steps.body: By patient, plan or step; and by state — in progress, stalled, finished, cancelled.

steps.title: New plan
steps.body: Built rather than typed: steps come from the patient’s chart and from the treatment catalogue.

steps.title: A plan
steps.body: Shows whose it is, how many steps are done and what the next one is. Press to open it.

steps.title: Stalled
steps.body: Nothing done and nothing booked for weeks. This is the whole reason the screen is sorted the way it is.

steps.title: Record a call
steps.body: Rang them and agreed to speak again in a month? Say so, and the plan stops being flagged until that day.

plans.example: A four-step plan for a root canal has had one visit in nine weeks. It shows at the top of the list marked Stalled. You ring, they ask for the new year, you record the call with a date — and it goes quiet until January.
tips: Stopping a plan does not erase it. Everything on it stays on the patient’s record and it can be reopened at any time.
A plan you write often can be started from one you wrote before, steps and all.

planDetail.title: A treatment plan
planDetail.tagline: The steps, in the order they will be done
planDetail.what: One agreed course of treatment. Steps are ticked off as they happen, booked into the calendar, reordered when the mouth disagrees with the plan, and printed for the patient to take home.

steps.title: The plan and its progress
steps.body: Whose it is, what it is called, and how far along it has got.

steps.title: The steps
steps.body: In order. Each carries the tooth it belongs to when it came from the chart, and shows whether it is booked.

steps.title: Ticking one off
steps.body: Done, or skipped, with the day it happened. A step can always be put back.

steps.title: Adding a step
steps.body: From the chart, from the treatment catalogue, or typed. Steps can be dragged into a different order.

planDetail.example: A three-visit plan is agreed on Monday. You press “Book the run”, ask for every two weeks at the same time of day, and the app finds three slots — skipping the day the practice is closed — in one go.
tips: Print it. A patient who leaves with the plan on paper is a patient who knows how many visits they agreed to.
A step booked into the calendar carries the plan with it, so the appointment already knows what it is for.

works.title: Works register
works.tagline: Everything sent out to a laboratory
works.what: Crowns, bridges, dentures — anything made outside the practice. The register says what went where, when it was promised back, and whether it has come.

steps.title: Search and filter
steps.body: By name, telephone, the laboratory’s serial number, the span or the kind of work; and by month, laboratory or state.

steps.title: New case
steps.body: Copy the laboratory’s docket into the register. One row per piece of work, with how many elements it carries.

steps.title: A case
steps.body: Who it is for, what is being made, by whom, when it went and when it is due back.

steps.title: Still out or back
steps.body: A case past its promised date shows as late. Mark it back the day it arrives and it leaves the chasing list.

steps.title: The docket
steps.body: Print a docket to go in the box with the impression — shade, type of work, stages and dates.

works.example: A zirconia crown for tooth 46 goes out on the 3rd, promised back on the 17th. On the 18th the register shows it one day late; the laboratory’s number is one press away on the follow-up board.
tips: Name your laboratories and your kinds of work once, under this section — then every case picks from a list rather than being spelt three different ways.
The front desk can read this register but not write it, which is what lets them answer “is my crown back yet” without opening a chart.

workProcedures.title: Kinds of work
workProcedures.what: The work this practice sends out — a crown, a bridge, a denture, a repair. Naming them here is what stops one kind of work becoming three spellings of itself in the register.

steps.title: The list
steps.body: Every kind of work the register can offer. Short by design.

steps.title: Add
steps.body: A name and nothing else. Add them all in one sitting.

steps.title: Suggestions
steps.body: Names typed onto cases before this list existed. Keep the one you mean; the rest are usually the same work written differently.

workProcedures.example: The register has “Zirconia crown”, “zirkon crown” and “Zr crown” typed on old cases. You add “Zirconia crown” once, and from then on every case picks it from the list.
tips: This list is only about naming. It changes nothing on cases already written.

labs.title: Laboratories
labs.tagline: Who the work goes to, and how to reach them
labs.what: The outside firms the practice sends cases to. The name goes on every case; the telephone number is what the follow-up board dials when something is late.

steps.title: The list
steps.body: Every laboratory named, with its number and how many cases are with it.

steps.title: Add one
steps.body: The name as the practice refers to them, and the number somebody actually rings.

steps.title: Notes
steps.body: Whose name to ask for, which days they collect — whatever gets it right the first time.

labs.example: A bridge is four days late. You open the follow-up, press the laboratory’s number, and speak to the person whose name is written in the notes — instead of hunting for a card in a drawer.
tips: A laboratory with no number on file is a laboratory somebody has to look up every time a case runs late.

prescriptions.title: Standard wording
prescriptions.tagline: Written once, read out for years
prescriptions.what: The templates prescriptions are written from. This screen is the wording, not the prescriptions themselves — what has actually been issued is a screen of its own.

steps.title: The templates
steps.body: Everything the practice writes often, grouped so the list stays short.

steps.title: Add one
steps.body: A name to pick it by, and the wording itself: dose, how often, and what to do if it gets worse.

steps.title: After a treatment
steps.body: Attach a template to the treatments it usually follows, and it is offered first when one of them has just been recorded.

prescriptions.example: You attach the post-extraction wording to “Extraction”. From then on, the moment an extraction is recorded, that wording is the first thing offered — with the patient’s name and the date already filled in.
tips: The wording is a starting point, never a straitjacket. It is edited freely for each patient before it is issued.
Prescribing is the dentist’s own act. Assistants can read prescriptions; only the dentist writes them.

prescriptionsIssued.title: Issued prescriptions
prescriptionsIssued.tagline: What the practice has actually written
prescriptionsIssued.what: Every prescription that has left the building, newest first, searched by patient. This is the record — the templates screen is only the wording it was written from.

steps.title: Search
steps.body: By patient name, which is the only name anybody looking for a prescription has.

steps.title: A prescription
steps.body: Who it was for, what was on it, who wrote it and when.

steps.title: Print again
steps.body: A patient who has lost theirs can be given the same sheet again without it being rewritten.

prescriptionsIssued.example: A patient rings on Sunday to say they have lost the antibiotics slip. You search their surname, open Friday’s prescription, and print the same one — no rewriting, no guessing at the dose.
tips: Every prescription is checked against the patient’s recorded allergies as it is written. That check is only as good as the alerts on their record.

inbox.title: Inbox
inbox.what: Replies from patients, gathered into conversations. It is the one queue here whose size nobody controls — a patient answers when they answer, and a reply nobody sees for three days is worse than a recall nobody makes for three days.

steps.title: Conversations
steps.body: Unread first. Each is a thread with one person, not a pile of loose messages.

steps.title: Linking to a patient
steps.body: A reply from an address nobody recognises is not attached to anybody. Link it once, and the conversation appears on their record for good.

steps.title: Reading a thread
steps.body: The whole exchange in order, including what the practice sent in the first place.

steps.title: Reply, or file it away
steps.body: Answer from here, or file the conversation when it is finished. Filed is not deleted.

inbox.example: A reminder goes out on Tuesday. On Wednesday “can we make it Thursday instead?” arrives. You link it to the patient, move the appointment, and reply — and the whole exchange is on their file.
tips: Nothing can arrive here until an email provider is set up. Until then the screen says so rather than looking broken.
The front desk can read and answer the inbox. It is mostly “can we move it”, which is their job, not the dentist’s.

requests.title: Requests from the website
requests.tagline: People who are not patients yet
requests.what: Somebody left their name and number on the practice’s public page. This is the only queue here where nobody has any relationship with the practice yet — a day of silence does not read as a delay, it reads as being ignored.

steps.title: The queue
steps.body: Oldest first, deliberately. The one who has waited longest is the one to ring.

steps.title: What they said
steps.body: Their name, their number, and whatever they wrote about what they need.

steps.title: Ring them back
steps.body: The number is a press away. There is no messaging here — this is a telephone call.

steps.title: Turn it into a booking
steps.body: Once a time is agreed, the request becomes a patient and an appointment in one step.

requests.example: A request comes in on Saturday: “broken tooth, any time next week”. Monday at nine the desk rings, books Tuesday afternoon, and the request closes itself as the appointment is made.
tips: The count in the navigation is a person waiting for a call, which is why it is one of only two numbers in the whole menu.

followUps.title: Follow-ups
followUps.what: The practice’s own to-do board: ring the laboratory, chase an invoice, order the thing nobody wrote down. Anything that has to happen on a day that is not today, and that would otherwise live on a sticky note.

steps.title: The counts
steps.body: How much is open and how much is late. The same numbers ride on the bell in the corner of every screen.

steps.title: The sections
steps.body: Late, today, this week, later, ticked off. Nothing has to be sorted by hand.

steps.title: A line
steps.body: What needs doing, when it should surface, and whose job it is — or anybody’s, which is the honest answer most of the time.

steps.title: Done, or later
steps.body: Tick it off, or push it a few days. Pushing is not failing; it is what stops the board filling with things nobody will do today.

followUps.example: Wednesday you write “ring Dentaland about the Berisha bridge”, due Friday. It stays out of the way until Friday morning, when it appears in the bell with a red mark against it.
tips: Marking one urgent puts it at the top and keeps it there. Use it sparingly, or the top stops meaning anything.
A late case in the works register can be turned into a follow-up with the laboratory’s number already attached.

recalls.title: Recalls
recalls.what: People the practice has not seen for as long as their own record says it should have. Two lists: those due a check-up, and those worth following up after recent treatment.

steps.title: The counts
steps.body: How many are overdue and how many are worth a call after treatment.

steps.title: Due for a check-up
steps.body: Their recall interval has passed and nothing is booked. Somebody with an appointment already is never on this list.

steps.title: A patient
steps.body: When they were last seen, how long that is, and how to reach them.

steps.title: Contact, or remind me later
steps.body: Prepare a reminder, or push them a few days if now is a bad time to ring.

recalls.example: A patient with a six-month recall was last in eleven months ago and has nothing booked. They appear here; you queue a reminder, it goes out with tomorrow’s batch, and they ring back on Thursday.
tips: The interval lives on each patient’s record. A patient set to “Never” is never chased, which is sometimes exactly right.
Reminders prepared here do not send themselves. They wait under Reminders to send until somebody presses the button.

outbox.title: Reminders to send
outbox.what: The queue of messages waiting to go out — mostly tomorrow’s appointment reminders. Nothing leaves this practice until a person presses send, which is the whole reason the screen exists.

steps.title: The counts
steps.body: Waiting, missed, and handled today.

steps.title: Waiting to be sent
steps.body: Tomorrow’s appointments with nobody told yet. This is the list to clear once a day.

steps.title: A reminder
steps.body: Who it is for, which appointment, and by which route — WhatsApp, email, or a telephone call.

steps.title: Send, or deal with it
steps.body: Send it, or mark it handled if it was settled another way.

outbox.example: At half past five you open this screen, see six reminders for tomorrow, and send five. The sixth has no number on file, so you mark it handled and ring the mother instead.
tips: “Nobody got to these” is the honest section: appointments that have already started and were never mentioned. It is short on a good week.
A patient who has asked not to be contacted never appears here, whatever is booked.

services.title: Services
services.tagline: What the practice offers, and for how long
services.what: The treatment catalogue. Every booking, every plan step and every price the practice quotes comes from this list, which is why it is worth getting right once.

steps.title: Search and filter
steps.body: By name, or by the department it is filed under.

steps.title: Add a treatment
steps.body: A name and a duration are enough. The duration is what the diary blocks out whenever it is booked.

steps.title: A treatment
steps.body: Its name, its department, how long it takes and what it costs.

steps.title: Materials it uses
steps.body: Say what a treatment normally spends, and recording the visit takes it off the shelf automatically.

services.example: “Composite filling — 45 minutes” is added once. From then on every filling booked blocks three quarters of an hour in the diary without anybody having to remember.
tips: Getting the durations right is what makes the calendar’s free-time finder useful. A 20-minute treatment booked as an hour hides slots that exist.
An existing price list can be brought in from a spreadsheet rather than typed — see Import.

serviceCategories.title: Service categories
serviceCategories.tagline: The departments the catalogue is filed by
serviceCategories.what: The parts of the practice a treatment can belong to — surgery, orthodontics, hygiene. Named once here so one department cannot become three spellings of itself.

steps.title: The list
steps.body: Departments, and the subdivisions inside them. Two levels deep and no further, on purpose.

steps.title: Add one
steps.body: A name, and whether it sits inside a department or is one.

steps.title: What uses it
steps.body: Every treatment picks its department from this list, and the catalogue is filtered by it.

serviceCategories.example: You add “Surgery” with “Extractions” and “Implants” inside it. The service list can then be narrowed to implants alone when quoting one.
tips: Do this before importing a price list. Names that already exist are matched instead of duplicated.

imports.title: Import from a spreadsheet
imports.what: A practice adopting this app already has lists — a price list, a storage-room inventory, a patient file. This brings them in from a CSV file, and shows exactly what it will do before it does anything.

steps.title: The file
steps.body: A CSV exported from a spreadsheet. The first row should be the column names.

steps.title: Matching the columns
steps.body: Say which column is the name, which is the price, and so on. The app guesses and you correct it.

steps.title: The preview
steps.body: Row by row: what will be added, what will be updated, and what cannot be read. Nothing has happened yet at this point.

steps.title: Import
steps.body: Only when you press this. Rows with problems are left out rather than guessed at.

imports.example: A price list of 180 treatments comes across in one go. The preview shows 174 new, 6 matching what is already there, and nothing broken — so you import, and the catalogue is done in a morning instead of a fortnight.
tips: Import is a once-per-practice errand, which is why it is filed under its section rather than sitting on the header for ever.
Materials import what each thing *is*, not how much of it is on the shelf. Count that with a stocktake.

stock.title: Stock
stock.tagline: The storage room, as a list
stock.what: Every material and consumable the practice keeps, how many are on the shelf, and how low each is allowed to get before the app starts asking for more.

steps.title: Search and filter
steps.body: By name, code, brand or shelf — and by whether something is low, out, or fine.

steps.title: Add a material
steps.body: A name and a count are enough. The shelf, the minimum and the supplier can wait.

steps.title: A material
steps.body: What it is, how many boxes are there, which shelf it lives on and who it is bought from.

steps.title: Low and out
steps.body: A material at or below its minimum joins the order list and is flagged in the bell on every screen.

steps.title: Add or take out
steps.body: Move stock without opening the record — a delivery in, a box used out.

stock.example: Anaesthetic has a minimum of 3 boxes. The nurse takes the second-to-last one, the count drops to 2, and by the time the dentist looks at the bell it is already on the order list.
tips: Every movement is written to a ledger with who did it and why, so “where did six boxes go” is an answerable question.
Lot numbers matter. A recall notice asks for the lot, and nothing else in the practice can answer it.

stockCatalog.title: Stock catalogue
stockCatalog.what: The same materials as the stock list, but with a photograph of each box. For anybody who knows what a thing looks like but not what it is called — which, with a new nurse and a shelf of Italian packaging, is most people.

steps.title: Search
steps.body: The same search as the list. Type what you can remember.

steps.title: The cards
steps.body: A photograph, the name, the shade or size, and how many are left.

steps.title: The photograph
steps.body: Press it to take or choose one. A variant with no photograph of its own shows the product’s.

steps.title: What is low
steps.body: A card carries the same low or out badge the list does.

stockCatalog.example: A locum needs “the composite in the blue box”. They open the catalogue, recognise the packaging in two seconds, and find that it is A2 on shelf 3.
tips: Photographs are worth an afternoon once. They pay for themselves every time somebody new works a shift.

stockLabels.title: Shelf labels
stockLabels.tagline: A QR code for every box
stockLabels.what: A printable sheet of labels, one per material. Stick them on the boxes, and moving stock becomes a matter of pointing a camera at a shelf rather than typing.

steps.title: The sheet
steps.body: Every material, or just the ones you filter to. It prints as a page of stickers.

steps.title: A label
steps.body: The name, the code, and a QR code that opens that material directly.

steps.title: Scanning one
steps.body: Opens the material with “add or take out” ready — choose how many boxes and press.

steps.title: Just one
steps.body: A single label can be printed on its own for a new material, without redoing the sheet.

stockLabels.example: A new shelf of composites is labelled on a Friday afternoon. On Monday the nurse takes three boxes out by scanning three stickers, and never opens the stock list at all.
tips: Labels are printed once per material and then not again for a year, which is why they live here rather than on the stock header.

stockScan.title: Scan
stockScan.tagline: Move stock by reading the box
stockScan.what: The fastest way to put a delivery away or take something off the shelf: read the code on the box, say how many, done. Works with the camera on a phone or with a handheld scanner.

steps.title: In or out
steps.body: A delivery adds to the shelf, with its lot number and expiry. Something used takes off the shelf, from the lot you scanned.

steps.title: Scanning
steps.body: Point the camera, or pull the trigger on a handheld reader — it works anywhere on this page without clicking first.

steps.title: Codes it does not know
steps.body: Say what an unknown code is once, and it is recognised from then on. A carton and a single box are different codes.

steps.title: The basket
steps.body: Everything scanned so far, ready to be corrected before it is saved.

stockScan.example: A delivery of twelve cartons arrives. The nurse scans each one, types the lot number and expiry once per product, and the whole delivery is on the shelf before the boxes are unpacked.
tips: Taking out more than the shelf says it holds is allowed — it happens, and the app tells you the count was already wrong rather than refusing.

stocktake.title: Count the shelf
stocktake.what: The reckoning: walk the storage room, type what you can see, and the app records the difference as a correction. Only the lines you change are recorded, so a count that is already right costs nothing.

steps.title: The list
steps.body: Every material with what the app believes is there. Filter to one shelf and work through it.

steps.title: Type what you see
steps.body: The real number. Leave the ones that are right alone — a blank means “no change”.

steps.title: The differences
steps.body: What will be corrected, and by how much, before anything is saved.

steps.title: Save
steps.body: Each correction is written to the ledger as a movement, signed, like everything else.

stocktake.example: A stocktake before the summer break finds gloves at 4 boxes when the app said 9. You type 4, save, and the correction is on the record with your name and the date — rather than five boxes quietly going missing.
tips: Doing this once a quarter is what keeps the low-stock alerts trustworthy. Alerts built on wrong counts get ignored, and then they are worth nothing.

stockExpiry.title: Expiry
stockExpiry.tagline: What has turned, and what is about to
stockExpiry.what: Lots past their date, and lots turning within the next few weeks. This is the screen that stops expired anaesthetic being found by a patient rather than by the practice.

steps.title: The counts
steps.body: How many lots have expired and how many are close.

steps.title: Expired
steps.body: Past their date, oldest first. These come off the shelf today.

steps.title: Expiring soon
steps.body: Still usable — use them first, or plan to replace them.

steps.title: Acting on a lot
steps.body: Take it off the shelf from here, and the movement is recorded like any other.

stockExpiry.example: Two lots of anaesthetic expire at the end of the month. They show under “expiring soon”, so the practice uses those first and the ones bought last week stay in the box.
tips: Expiry dates only exist for lots that were scanned or typed in with one. A material added without dates cannot warn anybody.

stockCategories.title: Stock categories
stockCategories.tagline: The shelves the storage room is filed by
stockCategories.what: The shelves, drawers and cupboards materials are filed under. Named once here, so one shelf does not become three spellings of itself across two hundred materials.

steps.title: The list
steps.body: Every shelf the storage room has. Short, and it stays short.

steps.title: Add one
steps.body: A name and nothing else. Add them all in one sitting.

steps.title: What uses it
steps.body: Every material picks its shelf from this list, and the stock list is filtered by it.

stockCategories.example: You add “Restoratives”, “Anaesthetics”, “Disposables” and “Endo”. Filtering the stock list to one shelf then matches the walk somebody actually takes around the room.
tips: Name them after where things physically are, not after what they theoretically belong to. The list is used while standing in the room.

suppliers.title: Suppliers
suppliers.tagline: Who the materials are bought from
suppliers.what: The firms the practice orders from. There is no ordering inside this app by design — this is the list of who to ring, attached to what they supply.

steps.title: The list
steps.body: Every supplier, with the number that actually gets an order placed.

steps.title: Add one
steps.body: A name is all that is needed, but the telephone number is the point of the record.

steps.title: Notes
steps.body: Whom to ask for, deliveries on which days, minimum order — whatever gets it right first time.

suppliers.example: The order list says four materials are low, and three are bought from the same firm. You open that supplier, ring the number on the record, and place one order instead of three.
tips: Point each material at its supplier. The suggested order list then groups itself by who to call.

analytics.title: Statistics
analytics.tagline: What the practice has been doing
analytics.what: The figures behind the work: how full the diary has been, which treatments come up most, how many people do not turn up, and what the practice has taken. Read over months, not days.

steps.title: The period
steps.body: Six months by default. Change it and everything on the screen follows.

steps.title: The headline figures
steps.body: The two or three numbers worth knowing before any chart is read.

steps.title: The charts
steps.body: Bookings and revenue over time, and which treatments make them up.

steps.title: The tables
steps.body: The same figures in rows, for anybody who would rather read numbers than shapes.

analytics.example: Chair utilisation reads 61% for the last six months. The chart shows Tuesdays are the hole; the practice moves a hygiene session there and watches the same number next quarter.
tips: Utilisation is booked minutes against the hours the practice was actually open — so wrong opening hours make it wrong.
The no-show figure excludes appointments the practice cancelled. It is about patients, not about the diary.

settings.title: Opening hours
settings.tagline: When the practice is open, and when it is shut
settings.what: The week the whole calendar is drawn from — opening times, the lunch break, holidays, and how many chairs can run at once. Almost everything else in the app that draws a day reads it from here.

steps.title: The week
steps.body: One row per day: when the doors open, when they close, and the break in the middle. Times are the clinic’s own clock.

steps.title: The times
steps.body: Leave a day empty and the practice is shut on it. The calendar greys it out immediately.

steps.title: Breaks and closures
steps.body: A break repeats every week; a closure is a holiday or a shutdown and overrides the week entirely.

steps.title: Save
steps.body: Nothing changes until you save — and if bookings already sit in hours you are closing, you are told before it happens.

settings.example: The practice starts closing on Saturdays. You empty Saturday’s two times, save, and every Saturday on the calendar greys out — and the free-slot finder stops offering them.
tips: Chairs are only worth adding if the practice really has more than one. Two chairs means two appointments can run at once.
One person’s leave is a closure for that person alone. The rest of the practice keeps working.

staff.title: Staff and roles
staff.tagline: Who works here, and what each may do
staff.what: The accounts people sign in with, and the role each one carries. A role is not a job title here — it is the set of doors that open, and it is the field worth pausing on.

steps.title: The list
steps.body: Everyone with an account, their role, and whether the account is still active.

steps.title: Add somebody
steps.body: A name, a role, and a PIN — told to them in person, not emailed.

steps.title: The role
steps.body: Everything a role grants is listed under it as you choose, so the decision is made with its consequences in view.

steps.title: Retiring an account
steps.body: Deactivate rather than delete. Their name stays on the visits they recorded, which is what a clinical record requires.

staff.example: A locum starts for three weeks. You give them Read-only: they can see charts, the diary and the figures, and cannot change a single thing — and every screen tells them so rather than refusing at the last moment.
tips: Deleting anything is the owner’s alone, deliberately. Everybody else cancels, deactivates or corrects.
Each person changes their own PIN from the account menu. Nobody, including the owner, can read anybody else’s.

activity.title: Activity log
activity.tagline: Every change, and who made it
activity.what: An append-only record of what was changed, by whom and when. Nothing here can be edited or removed, including by the owner — that is the entire point of keeping it.

steps.title: The entries
steps.body: Newest first: who, what, and which record it touched.

steps.title: Filter by type
steps.body: Narrow to one kind of change — bookings, patients, stock, staff.

steps.title: Date range
steps.body: Narrow to the days in question when there is a specific question.

steps.title: What it signs
steps.body: Every entry carries the account that made the change, which is why PINs are personal and never shared.

activity.example: A visit note says something nobody remembers writing. The log shows it was recorded at 16:20 on the 4th by a named account — and the question is answered in a minute rather than becoming an argument.
tips: Only the owner can read this, and nobody at all can change it.
Sharing a PIN makes every line this log writes worthless. That is the real reason each person has their own.

stockItem.title: A material
stockItem.tagline: One thing on the shelf, and everything that happened to it
stockItem.what: What this material is, how many boxes are there, which deliveries they came from, and every movement in and out with a name against it. This is where “where did six boxes go” is answered.

steps.title: Move it, or correct it
steps.body: Take some out or put a delivery in without leaving the record. Editing changes what the material is — its name, its shelf, its minimum.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body: The article number staff read off the box, the shelf it lives on, who it is bought from, and a photograph of the packaging.

steps.title: Expiry
steps.body: Red on a lot that has turned, amber on one turning soon. The oldest still-usable lot is the one to reach for.

steps.title: The lots
steps.body: Each delivery kept apart, with its lot number and the day it arrived — the number a recall notice asks for, and the only thing that can answer one.

steps.title: The ledger
steps.body: Every movement, with who made it and why. Nothing here is edited: a mistake is corrected by another movement, and both stay.

stockItem.example: The count says nine boxes of gloves and the shelf holds four. The ledger shows a stocktake correction of −5 last Tuesday with a name against it — so the question is answered in a minute instead of becoming an accusation.
tips: A lot recorded without an expiry date cannot warn anybody. Scanning a delivery in is the quickest way to capture one.
Correcting a count here writes a movement like any other. Nothing in this app changes a number without saying who and why.

stockOrders.title: Orders
stockOrders.tagline: What was ordered, and what actually arrived
stockOrders.what: The orders placed with suppliers, and the boxes still owed on each. The storage list can only say a material is on its way; this is what remembers that you asked for ten and six came.

steps.title: Open, or finished
steps.body: Open orders are what is still owed. The button in the corner switches to the ones that are complete or were given up on.

steps.title: An order
steps.body: Who it was placed with, the day it went out, and the day they said it would come.

steps.title: Late, and how much is left
steps.body: A red badge counts the days past the promised date. The teal one counts the boxes nobody has received yet.

steps.title: The lines
steps.body: One row per material: how many were asked for and how many have arrived. A line that is complete says so and stops being counted.

steps.title: Giving up on it
steps.body: Closes the order and stops waiting for the rest. Whatever did arrive stays on the shelf.

stockOrders.example: Ten boxes of gloves are ordered on the 3rd and promised for the 10th. Six arrive on the 9th. The order stays open showing four still owed, and on the 11th it starts counting days late — so the supplier gets a call about four boxes, rather than no call at all because everybody thought it had landed.
tips: Orders are placed from the suggested-order list on the storage page. This screen records them; nothing is sent from here.
No prices, deliberately. What an order cost is a business figure and lives with the statistics, which only the roles allowed to see money can open.
